newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia bourses see upturn, brokers eye rebellion.
newsitem.headline: Colombia bourses see upturn, brokers eye rebellion.

text.p: Falling interest rates, a more stable political climate and technological change will breathe new life into Colombia's dormant equities markets next year, leaders of the country's three stock exchanges said Tuesday.

But their upbeat predictions found little echo among brokers who are threatening to rebel against bourse authorities in 1997 if they continue to see their profit margins eroded by overregulated markets, high commission payments and officials' failure to help kickstart genuine supply and demand.
In his speech to the Stock Brokers Congress, Carlos Caballero, chairman of the Bogota exchange, admitted 1996 was "desperate".

The value of stock trades in Bogota, Medellin and the smaller Cali exchanges has fallen 35 percent in real terms in the year to date, while fixed-income volumes have remained about the same as last year, he said.

"There are a number of factors that lead us to believe 1997 could see an upturn in the markets. Interest rates have dropped and although the political climate is not completely clear, political factors have been assimilated by the markets," said Julian Dominguez, head of the Cali-based Western Exchange.

But he acknowledged that the practice of pre-arranged, pocket-to-pocket deals between shareholders in the country's large conglomerates could continue to stifle genuine supply and demand in the markets.
Central bank overnight interest rates are currently at 23 percent, while average fixed term deposit rates at the bank are running at around 28 percent, down 3 percentage points since June.
Caballero added that coupled with declining interest rates, the move to integrate the three stock exchanges into one market via a computer link-up would make for easier trading.
It could also revive interest from foreign funds, which he said were sometimes "unsure of the rules of the game" in Colombia.
Cali and Medellin are due to link up in February. No date has been announced for when Bogota could be connected to the network.
But the stated aims of the bourse chairmen have failed to make the move from the drawing board on to the trading floor.
"A lot of what has been mentioned here today will never trickle down to us," said Emilio Echavarria, chairman of the Medellin-based Suvalor brokerage.
"The situation is very difficult. The economic crisis makes for stagnant markets, and we're paying service rates to the bourse authorities of about 12 percent on commissions," he said.
Brokers are now looking to form an association, whose "interests would not always match those of the bourse authorities," Echavarria added.
Brokers were skeptical of bourse chief pledges to speed integration of the exchanges, and stressed that each market still tries to compete with the other two.
"We're suffering from the selfish attitudes of all three exchanges and high levels of inefficiency," one broker said.
